paragraphs: Five fostering services list Peterborough as an area they cover, among them Peterborough City Council's own fostering service, and they are shown above. The council says it most urgently needs homes for brothers and sisters who should stay together, children over 10 and teenagers, children with disabilities or complex health or emotional needs, and children who need a long-term family.

To foster for the council you need to be over 21 and have a spare bedroom. You can be retired, rent your home or be out of work, there is no upper age limit, and for most kinds of fostering working is not a barrier. The council asks for some experience of children, whether through work, volunteering or family life. Its process runs from enquiry and a home visit through a four-day training course and assessment to a fostering panel, and normally takes four to six months.

The council offers emergency care for up to 72 hours, time-limited care for up to two years, long-term fostering, respite, parent and baby placements and kinship care. Its Link scheme gives disabled children living at home regular short breaks, from one or two nights a month. Supported lodgings hosts, who offer a room to young people aged 16 to 21, are paid £250 a week while a young person lives with them. New carers are given an experienced carer as a mentor, a supervising social worker, local training, free Fostering Network membership, an employee assistance service and family membership of the city's Vivacity leisure centres.

Since autumn 2025 the council has run a Foster Friendly employer scheme, and Anglian Water, Nene Park Trust and Meridian Trust have joined it, giving staff who foster extra leave, usually up to five days a year, for meetings and training. Talk to the council and two or three of the services above, and see the Cambridgeshire page if you live outside the city.
